item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: MAGE: an efficient algorithm for identifying Maximal Age-indexed GEne sets
item.description: Abstract Aging alters transcriptional regulation in a tissue- and time-specific manner, reshaping gene regulatory networks and shifting regulatory influence dynamics. Traditional in silico influence maximization methods often rely on static gene expression snapshots and fail to capture gene-to-gene influence variations over time. To address this, we introduce the Age Index , a network-based metric that quantifies time-varying gene influence. We define the Maximal and Minimal Age Index Problems (MAP$^{+}$ and MAP$^{-}$) as the tasks of identifying gene sets with the highest and lowest Age Index, and prove these problems are NP-hard. To solve them, we develop MAGE (Maximal Age-Index Algorithm), a stochastic method that iteratively constructs gene sets by prioritizing genes likely to optimize the Age Index. MAGE identifies statistically significant gene sets at the genome scale, with strong literature support, highlighting its potential to uncover age-sensitive regulatory mechanisms.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: HiCP2GAN: a plug and play foundation model-based GAN for Hi-C enhancement
item.description: Abstract The 3D organization of chromatin shapes gene regulation and cellular function, and Hi-C has become the primary technique for mapping chromatin interactions genome-wide. However, high-resolution data remain costly and scarce, leaving many studies with sparse contact maps that limit downstream analysis. Deep learning methods, especially generative adversarial networks (GANs), have shown promise for enhancing low-resolution Hi-C data, but most existing GAN-based approaches rely on custom discriminators trained from scratch, which can yield unstable training and limited generalization. Hi-C foundation models pretrained on large-scale data capture rich, transferable representations of chromatin structure, yet their use as discriminators within adversarial enhancement frameworks had not been explored. We introduce HiCP2GAN, a plug-and-play GAN that employs a pretrained Vision Transformer-based Hi-C foundation model as its discriminator. The discriminator was pretrained on 118 million Hi-C patches across diverse species and cell types, providing biologically meaningful gradients for adversarial supervision. The framework is generator-agnostic: any compatible Hi-C resolution enhancement architecture can serve as the generator, enabling fair comparison across methods. The encoder phase of the foundation model was adapted as a discriminator backbone, finetuning the first few layers from the input while freezing the deeper transformer layers to preserve pretrained knowledge while allowing task-specific adaptation. Experiments across various cell lines show that HiCP2GAN outperforms traditional GAN-based methods in most settings and improves the reconstruction quality and biological reproducibility of existing Hi-C enhancement models in most evaluated cases. HiCP2GAN is publicly available at https://github.com/OluwadareLab/HiCP2GAN .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: IsoPrism predicts isoform usage from short-read transcriptomes through structure-guided competitive allocation
item.description: Abstract Short-read (SR) single-cell and spatial transcriptomics characterize gene expression but provide limited resolution of within-gene isoform usage. Here we present IsoPrism, a structure-guided competitive allocation framework that predicts isoform proportions from gene-level expression. IsoPrism combines individual expression and local expression context with transcript structural annotations, using shared iterative updates to preserve non-negative, gene-normalized proportions. Joint supervision from individual long-read (LR) counts and group-level isoform usage enables prediction in samples without matched LR measurements. Across five transfer scenarios derived from three paired transcriptomic resources, IsoPrism achieved the highest mean dominant isoform accuracy, compositional similarity, and cluster-level allocation correlation among eight evaluated methods. Ablation analyses supported complementary contributions from structural queries, expression context, iterative allocation, and dual-resolution supervision. Applied to a developing mouse cortex atlas, IsoPrism identified stage- and cell-type-associated isoform-usage patterns, including variation in the predicted relative usage of two Pkm transcripts. IsoPrism enables isoform-usage analysis of SR transcriptomes by transferring information from paired LR references, extending the analytical value of existing single-cell and spatial gene-expression atlases.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: ADInteractome: discovering Alzheimer’s disease-associated gene interactions from single-nucleus RNA-seq data through neural interaction states
item.description: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid $\beta $ plaques and tau tangles, yet its molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Advances in single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) have provided profound insights into the cellular heterogeneity of AD-associated brains. In this study, we introduce ADInteractome, an interpretable artificial intelligence framework designed to discover gene interactions associated with AD directly from the internal state of neural networks trained on the snRNA-seq data of brain cells. The method is based on the intuition that if a neural network can accurately classify cells from AD and non-AD donors based on their snRNA-seq data, then its internal interaction states, reflecting interaction patterns within the gene expression data, are informative for identifying biologically meaningful gene interactions. Applied to a large-scale snRNA-seq dataset from the Seattle Alzheimer’s Disease Brain Cell Atlas, ADInteractome reveals cell-type-specific and AD-associated gene circuits supported by existing literature. The results were further supported by our virtual knock-out and knock-in experiments, a novel concept to probe our findings through a data-driven approach. Compared with traditional co-expression network methods, it achieves stronger enrichment for known AD-associated gene interactions and uncovers novel interaction patterns. These findings highlight the potential of interpretable AI approaches for elucidating complex molecular interactions in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Multi-omics survival prediction under modality incompleteness via dynamic modality graphs and product-of-experts fusion
item.description: Abstract Multi-omics data integration provides rich complementary information for cancer survival prediction, yet modality incompleteness is pervasive in real-world medical data and undermines the stability and applicability of existing models. To address this challenge, we propose DMG-PoE, a robust learning framework for multi-omics survival prediction. The framework introduces a dynamic modality graph (DMG) that propagates complementary information across modality nodes to compensate for missing inputs, combined with an uncertainty-aware product-of-experts (PoE) fusion mechanism that adaptively weights each modality by its estimated precision, and a consistency-constrained training strategy that stabilizes predictions across varying modality subsets. Systematic evaluation on the SurvBoard benchmark across 10 TCGA cancer types and seven omics modalities demonstrates that DMG-PoE achieves the highest average C-index under both the standard setting (complete-modality training/testing) and the missing-augmented setting (training additionally includes real incomplete samples and nonclinical modality dropout, with complete-only testing); controlled per-modality masking experiments validate effective test-time recovery in 22/24 cancer-modality combinations, and cross-cohort transfer with only two of seven modalities available further confirms generalization under severe input restriction.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C
item.description: Abstract Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%–80% fewer trainable parameters (113K–137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

item.title: Bioinformatics: Assessment of LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and code writing
item.description: Abstract Motivation Large Language Models (LLMs), AI agents and co-scientists promise to accelerate scientific discovery across fields ranging from chemistry to biology. Bioinformatics—the analysis of DNA, RNA and protein sequences plays a crucial role in biological research and is especially amenable to AI-driven automation given its computational nature. Here, we assess the bioinformatics capabilities of popular general-purpose LLMs on a set of tasks covering basic analytical questions that include code writing and multi-step reasoning in the domain. Results Utilizing questions from Rosalind, a bioinformatics educational platform, we compare the performance of the LLMs on 104 questions relative to expert ground truth and 68 760 humans with varying levels of expertise. Among the frontier LLMs evaluated (GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3-70B, Llama-4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6), GPT-5.2 exhibited top performance, providing correct answers for 80/104 (77%) questions followed by Claude Sonnet 4.6. LLM performance varied widely depending on the biological categories of questions. While the latest generation of frontier LLM models showed overall improvements in performance, their performance in specific categories of biological questions was lower than first generation models. Overall, LLMs performance mirrored that of humans with lower performance in tasks in which humans had low performance and vice versa. However, LLMs also failed in some instances where most humans were correct and, in a few cases, LLMs excelled where most humans failed. To the best of our knowledge, this presents the first assessment of general purpose LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks in distinct areas relative to both expert and non-expert ground truths. Availability and Implementation The complete analysis was implemented in Python; all code is available at https://github.com/SiwoResearch/lllm-bioinformatics .

item.title: Bioinformatics: pxGPT: a schema-constrained multimodal large language model framework for plant phenotyping
item.description: Abstract Summary Deep learning can scale image-based plant phenotyping but typically targets predefined traits, whereas manual phenotypic description is more flexible but difficult to scale. We present Phenotype eXplorer Generative Plant Traits (pxGPT), a Python framework that converts multi-view plant images into structured phenotype records. The workflow combines free-text description, dataset-specific schema generation with human review, and schema-constrained information extraction. We evaluated the extraction stage on three Brassica datasets using 78 973 annotations from 10 annotators who had no access to pxGPT predictions. For 38–45 qualitative traits per dataset, pxGPT-human agreement ranged from 0.572 to 0.712, compared with 0.620 to 0.739 agreement among human annotators. All 32 736 required trait fields were present; 93 values were empty, and no qualitative descriptor violations were recorded. For selected morphological structures, pooled false-positive rates were 0.5%–8.0%, while sensitivity varied across structure types in one mature-plant dataset (37.5%–100%). The curated schemas were applied unchanged with two commercial models and one locally hosted open-weight model, with differences in mean accuracy of 0.03 or less. In the evaluated Brassica datasets, these results support schema-guided extraction of visible plant traits without separate model training for each trait. Human-guided schema development offers a path to extend pxGPT to other crops and imaging conditions, with accuracy requiring validation in each new setting. Availability and implementation The software is available at https://github.com/YaoChengLab/pxgpt and an archival version of the source code is available on Zenodo ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22931745 ). Curated schemas used in this study, annotation guides, phenotype records, and human annotations are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907554 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: ct-validation: an open framework for benchmarking target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes
item.description: Abstract Summary Human genetic evidence provides a strong foundation for selecting drug targets. However, consistent benchmarking of target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes has been hindered by proprietary data and customized pipelines. To address this, we present the Python package ct-validation, which evaluates whether target-indication pairs supported by specific evidence sources are enriched for clinical progression. This package computes relative success (RS) and odds ratios with confidence intervals across clinical phase transitions. It also supports ontology-based semantic disease matching and offers interfaces in Python, on the command line, and via the Model Context Protocol. By remapping the benchmark from Minikel et al. (2024) to the Experimental Factor Ontology, we reproduced their per-transition enrichment, with a maximum difference of only 1.4% across any transition. In a systematic 3 × 3 benchmark that independently varies the genetic evidence and clinical trial sources, we found that a single curated open clinical trial source reproduces the signal of the proprietary comparator (RS = 2.92 versus 2.65; 2.34 versus 2.55 without oncology). However, aggregating open clinical trial registries compresses this signal (RS = 1.52); this loss is primarily driven by the breadth of the indication data rather than the genetic evidence. Availability and implementation ct-validation is implemented in Python (version 3.11 or higher), distributed via pip, and freely available at https://github.com/gero-science/ct-validation , with support for Python, command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901497 . Benchmark data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901451

item.title: Bioinformatics: Integration of polygenic risk with single cell methylation data using met-scDRS
item.description: Abstract Motivation Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism for their risk is through cellular context-dependent epigenetics such as methylation. Previous methodologies have focused on integrating GWAS with single cell transcriptomics, which allowed identification of within-cell-type heterogeneity in disease risk association. We extended this framework to provide a method called met-scDRS that integrates GWAS with single cell epigenomics and investigates how psychiatric disease risk can manifest through methylomics at single cell resolution. Results We propose an approach that integrates single cell methylomes with disease associated genes identified from GWAS at single-cell resolution. We found our method to be well calibrated and powered in different scenarios. We then analysed a publicly available single cell methylome dataset of the human brain for 75 different traits and generated disease relevance scores for each cell for each trait. We find high brain specificity with major cell type enrichments congruent with known findings. We identify within-cell-type heterogeneity for psychiatric disease risk along the brain spatial axis as well as subpopulations that are differentially associated with diseases. Finally, we showed that genes with high correlation between methylation levels and disease relevance scores to be highly enriched in specific functional pathways such as synaptic formation and transmission. Availability met-scDRS is freely available in GitHub as a python package under MIT license: https://github.com/bogdanlab/met-scDRS . Source code is also available from Zenodo with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21841506. All dataset used in this work are publicly available.

item.title: Bioinformatics: MR-MAS: an end-to-end multi-agent system for autonomous Mendelian randomization analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses. Results We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research. Availability and Implementation The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS , with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: MARDy 2.0: a platform for exploring and analysing antifungal resistance mutations
item.description: Abstract Motivation The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control. Results We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualizing mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR. Availability and implementation Accessible at https://mardy.net .

item.title: Bioinformatics: DNA-BFN: Bayesian flow networks for generative modeling of regulatory DNA sequences
item.description: Abstract Motivation Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. Results Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. Availability and implementation The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN . The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: FMCerNet: frequency-aware multi-label learning for fine-grained cervical cytology screening
item.description: Abstract Motivation Automated cytology screening is essential for early cervical cancer prevention, where gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) are typically partitioned into tiles for tile-level feature extraction and subsequent WSI-level diagnosis aggregation. However, existing tile-level methods remain constrained by limited input sizes, which frequently obscures sparse and morphologically subtle abnormal cells. Furthermore, these methods commonly formulate tile-level representation learning as a coarse single-label classification task, thereby failing to capture the complex co-occurrence patterns and morphological heterogeneity of cervical cytological abnormalities. Results We propose the Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning Network (FMCerNet), a tile-level feature extractor equipped with a Large-Field Frequency-Enhanced ViT backbone and a Coarse-to-Fine multi-label classification head. The former incorporates a Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform module to efficiently extract frequency-domain features from large-scale tiles, whereas the latter enhances fine-grained tile representation decoding through hierarchical supervision. Experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate that FMCerNet improves the accuracy of positive screening and fine-grained subtype classification while maintaining high inference speed. Availability and implementation Code at https://github.com/imAzhou/FMCerNet and archived on Zenodo (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.22886105).

item.title: Bioinformatics: Deepweed: automated individual segmentation and tracking for duckweed lineage analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Aquatic duckweeds, including Wolffia australiana , are the smallest and fastest growing flowering plants on the planet, with numerous emerging biotechnological applications. Duckweed populations grow through rapid clonal budding, but existing phenotypic characterization and image analysis tools typically operate only at the population level, tracking neither individual plants nor their lineage structure. Deepweed addresses this gap, combining automated individual segmentation, temporal tracking, and clonal lineage reconstruction from time-lapse imaging of duckweed. Results Deepweed processes time-lapse duckweed imaging datasets using deep-learning–based instance segmentation and multi-object tracking to assign persistent identities to individual fronds and infer mother–daughter relationships. The workflow outputs lineage graphs, individual-level morphological metrics, and population-level growth summaries, supported by lineage-annotated time-lapse visualizations. Applied to dense Wolffia populations, in both freely growing or controlled microfluidic environments, our framework can track hundreds of Wolffia plants simultaneously, resolves overlapping individuals, and reconstructs multi-generation lineage structure, enabling analyses that are inaccessible with population-level phenotyping methods. Availability Deepweed is implemented in Python using PyTorch, scikit-image, OpenCV, and btrack. Source code, trained models, example datasets, and documentation are freely available at https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/Deepweed . The Deepweed code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844282 and the datasets are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18843917 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Seq2Pocket: augmenting protein language models for spatially consistent binding site prediction
item.description: Abstract Motivation Protein–ligand binding site prediction (LBS) is important for many areas of structural biology and molecular modeling, where, as in other tasks, protein language models (pLMs) have shown great promise. In their application to LBS, the pLM classifies each amino acid as binding or not, but translating these predictions into three-dimensional binding pockets remains challenging; in particular, residue-centric predictions tend to produce spatially fragmented pockets. Results We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing. First, we introduce sc-PDB enhanced , an extended training dataset that augments an existing sc-PDB dataset with additional small-molecule and ion-binding sites, improving coverage of non-obvious and small pockets. Second, we employ an embedding-supported smoothing classifier to refine residue-level predictions. Third, we define the Pocket Fragmentation Index and use it to select a clustering approach that preserves a consistent mapping between predictions and ground-truth pockets. We evaluate Seq2Pocket on two tasks: general binding site prediction using the LIGYSIS benchmark and cryptic binding site prediction using CryptoBench benchmark. Across both benchmarks, Seq2Pocket achieves state-of-the-art DCC top-N and DCC top-(N + 2) performance. In particular, for general binding site prediction on the LIGYSIS benchmark, it improves distance-center-to-center recall by up to 13%, outperforming existing predictors. This improvement originates from training data quality rather than model architecture, as demonstrated by an ablation study. We believe that these findings contribute to more reliable evaluation practices in ligand binding site prediction, highlight the importance of training data curation, and provide pocket-level prediction tools that are better suited for downstream applications such as drug discovery. Availability The Seq2Pocket web interface is available at https://seq2pocket.projekty.ms.mff.cuni.cz , running the ESM-2 650M variant. The sc-PDB enhanced is published using Zenodo platform at https://zenodo.org/records/18271517 . The models are published at HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/skrhakv/seq2pocket .

item.title: Bioinformatics: DNAharvester: a nextflow pipeline for analysing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens
item.description: Abstract Motivation Ancient DNA (aDNA) research has advanced rapidly with the development of high-throughput sequencing, enabling genome-wide analyses of large collections of prehistoric specimens. However, analysing palaeontological and archaeological material with highly degraded DNA constitutes a major bioinformatic challenge. DNA from such samples is characterized by short fragment lengths, low endogenous content, post-mortem damage, and cross-species contamination, which can increase spurious mapping and reference bias, affecting downstream population genetic inferences. Results We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens. DNAharvester integrates metagenomic filtering, competitive mapping, adaptive aligner selection (incorporating BWA-aln , BWA-mem , and Bowtie2 ), and systematic evaluation of reference bias and spurious mapping. By incorporating flexible mapping and filtering strategies, the pipeline can be adapted to varying sample preservation, focusing on maximizing authentic data recovery. DNAharvester features subworkflows for iterative assembly of mitogenomes, identification of genomic repeats and CpG sites, taxonomic classification, microbial/pathogen screening, genetic sex determination, and variant calling. To accommodate varying sequencing depths, the pipeline supports diploid variant calling, genotype likelihood estimation, and pseudo-haploid random allele calling. We validated the pipeline using simulated and empirical datasets, demonstrating its ability to systematically mitigate complex background contamination while preserving authentic genomic signals. By streamlining complex bioinformatic tasks through simple configuration files, DNAharvester establishes a standardized approach for analysing aDNA datasets and makes genomic analyses of ancient remains accessible to the broader research community. Availability and Implementation Implemented in Nextflow, DNAharvester provides a highly scalable, containerized framework that enhances reproducibility, portability, and robustness in aDNA analyses. DNAharvester is open source under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and freely available at https://github.com/NBISweden/DNAharvester .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Motion-corrected Noise2Noise denoising for structural analysis of cells and tissues with (cryo-)FIB/SEM
item.description: Abstract Motivation (Cryo-)FIB/SEM enables 3D ultrastructural analysis of cells and tissues at nanoscale resolution. However, its characteristically low signal-to-noise ratio severely hinders interpretation of the volume data. Noise2Noise (N2N) has emerged as a state-of-the-art denoising paradigm with outstanding performance in 3D electron microscopy—particularly cryo-ET—but its direct application to (cryo-)FIB/SEM remains unfeasible due to the inherent acquisition workflows. Results A method to enable N2N denoising in (cryo-)FIB/SEM is introduced. The input volume is split into even and odd slices, followed by the application of motion correction methods to estimate and compensate for the structural differences between the two subvolumes. The resulting motion-corrected subvolumes are then used to train the N2N model, which is ultimately applied to denoise the original volume. Representative (cryo-)FIB/SEM volumes have been used to validate the method and to demonstrate the critical importance of the motion correction stage for volumes with a slice thickness >10 nm. Availability and implementation Code is available at https://github.com/microscopy-processing/N2N-REO and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22303478 .
