item.title: Bioinformatics: ScopeNovo: a de novo peptide sequencing method using spectrum–spectrum similarity to refine the prediction accuracy
item.description: Abstract Motivation De novo peptide sequencing from tandem mass spectra is essential for characterizing unknown proteins, identifying novel post-translational modifications, and analysing samples without reference databases. While recent deep learning models have improved the predicted peptide accuracy, they typically select the predicted peptide sequence based solely on sequence-level decoding scores. Very often, high scores are assigned to peptides without the direct support from the observed mass spectrum. Results We present “ScopeNovo”, a de novo peptide sequencing method that improves predicted peptide accuracy by using spectrum-spectrum similarity between the input spectrum and the “representative” spectrum corresponding to the predicted peptide sequence. ScopeNovo generates multiple candidate peptides using an existing peptide de novo sequencing learning model and reranks candidates based on spectrum–spectrum similarity. To test our method, we use π-PrimeNovo as the base learning model. Experimental results on the standard nine-species benchmark datasets V1 and V2 show that ScopeNovo can substantially improve the prediction accuracy. We designed two settings, where Setting 1 is for well-annotated species, and Setting 2 is for species that are not well annotated. For Setting 1, ScopeNovo improves the average peptide accuracies of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 6.1% and 4.0% on V1 and V2, respectively. For Setting 2, ScopeNovo can still improve the peptide accuracy of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 3.4% and 1.9% on the V1 and V2 benchmark datasets, respectively. Compared to the best-known method, RankNovo, the peptide accuracies over the nine species on V1 and V2 of our method for Setting 1 are 0.711 and 0.737, where the peptide accuracies for RankNovo are 0.687 and 0.682. Even for Setting 2, the peptide accuracies of our method are comparable to those of RankNovo. Availability and implementation ScopeNovo is implemented in Python under an MIT license. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/SoSongzhi/ScopeNovo.git . The test data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23181841 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Ryder: epigenome normalization using a two-tier model and internal reference regions
item.description: Abstract Motivation Sequencing-based epigenomic profiling methods are powerful but suffer from technical variability that complicates cross-sample comparisons and can obscure true biological signals. While existing normalization methods using spike-in controls or computational approaches have been proposed, they often rely on assumptions that may not hold across diverse experimental conditions or require additional data types. Results We present Ryder, a flexible and robust Python package for the normalization of epigenomic signal tracks. Ryder leverages stable internal reference regions, such as invariant CTCF binding sites, to correct for technical artifacts genome-wide. Our results show that it effectively adjusts both background noise and signal intensity, ensuring accurate signal alignment across samples while preserving genuine biological differences. We demonstrate that Ryder performs robustly across diverse assays including DNase-seq, CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, MNase-seq, and ChIP-seq, with or without spike-in controls. By reducing technical noise, Ryder improves the detection of genuine biological changes, such as quantitative reduction of chromatin accessibility at key enhancer elements by depletion of BRG1, a key subunit of the chromatin remodeling BAF complexes. Availability and implementation The Ryder source code, documentation and test data are freely available at: https://github.com/YaqiangCao/ryder . The software version used in this study is archived at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21267457 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: PanRes: a database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search
item.description: Abstract Motivation Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations. Results We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity. Availability and implementation PanRes is available through an interactive web platform ( https://panres.rambio.dk/ ), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216).

item.title: Nature Methods: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics
item.description: This Article presents MassNet, a large-scale AI-ready corpus of 1.5 billion MS/MS spectra spanning 35 species, paired with a standardized storage format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT). Built on this resource, XuanjiNovo is a nonautoregressive transformer for de novo peptide sequencing that substantially outperforms previous methods.

item.title: Bioinformatics: CRISPR-HAWK: haplotype- and variant-aware guide design toolkit for CRISPR-Cas
item.description: Abstract Motivation Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations. Results We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79 648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing. Availability CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK .

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: In vivo engineering of CAR natural killer cells for immunotherapy using ligand-directed lipid nanoparticles
item.description: Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cells to treat autoimmune disease and cancer are generated in vivo.

item.title: Nature Methods: Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens
item.description: A small, photoswitchable and genetically encodable protein operating in the near-infrared window is reported for photoacoustic tomography applications.

item.title: Bioinformatics: CryoTriplane: triplane-based neural radiance field representation for high-resolution cryo-EM 3D homogeneous reconstruction
item.description: Abstract Motivation Determining the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins is a cornerstone of structural biology, providing essential insights into their underlying biological mechanisms and functional roles. Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis allows researchers to investigate biomolecules at near-atomic resolutions, unraveling the structure of biomolecular complexes. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D volumes from extremely noisy projections, particularly under the interference of structural heterogeneity, remains a challenging task. Traditional Fourier-domain methods often suffer from frequency-dependent signal attenuation and uneven information distribution. While recent deep-learning-based frameworks attempt to predict high-frequency components directly in frequency space, they are highly susceptible to noise and often introduce artifacts. State-of-the-art (SOTA) real-space method circumvents Fourier-domain defects, yet remains constrained by the inherent spectral bias of multi-layer perceptrons, as fixed positional encoding fails to sufficiently capture intricate high-frequency details. Results We propose cryoTriplane, a real-space 3D homogeneous reconstruction network that utilizes a hybrid spatial representation to adaptively capture fine structural details. By combining fixed positional encoding for noise-robust structural initialization with structure-aware positional encoding for high-frequency refinement, our method achieves 3D reconstructions that are simultaneously globally consistent and locally fine-grained. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations across five simulated and four real-world datasets demonstrate that cryoTriplane significantly outperforms existing methods in resolving fine structural features. Furthermore, validation through downstream atomic modeling underscores cryoTriplane’s ability to recover high-quality density maps. Specifically, our method achieves sequence coverage improvements of 4.6% and 5.5% on the EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10492 datasets over the SOTA approach, respectively. Availability and implementation Our code is available at https://github.com/chengyr1999/CryoTriplane . The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

item.title: Bioinformatics: Representation-aware conformal prediction for reliable uncertainty quantification in drug-target affinity
item.description: Abstract Motivation Quantifying predictive uncertainty is essential for computational drug discovery to reduce experimental costs and false positives. However, most drug-target affinity (DTA) models focus on improving prediction accuracy without reliable uncertainty estimates. Results We propose representation-aware conformal prediction (RCP)-DTA, a representation-aware conformal prediction framework that constructs adaptive prediction intervals based on feature similarity. By constructing local calibration sets, our approach generates sample-specific prediction intervals that achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal confidence level. To improve representation quality, RCP-DTA employs a cross-modal architecture that integrates pretrained sequence representations and structural information. Binding site context is incorporated via virtual pocket feedback to enhance residue representations, followed by gated fusion for adaptive integration of sequence and structural modalities. Evaluations across multiple DTA benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCP-DTA achieves competitive affinity prediction performance while providing reliable uncertainty quantification. Availability and implementation Code and data are available at: https://github.com/Lee515628/RCP-DTA

item.title: Bioinformatics: Efficient and scalable Python implementation of ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 for omics differential abundance testing
item.description: Abstract Summary Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) and its successor ANCOM-BC2 are critical algorithms for differential abundance analysis. Designed for handling compositional data, they feature the ability to estimate the unknown sampling fractions and correct the bias induced by their differences. While the original R package implementing the two methods is robust for standard dataset sizes, the increasing magnitude of modern multiomics studies presents computational challenges, often resulting in a runtime bottleneck for high-dimensional data. Here, we present native Python implementations of both ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 in the scikit-bio package, significantly accelerating the workflow and enabling their application to large-scale datasets. By leveraging vectorization with NumPy and numerical optimization in SciPy, we enhanced the efficiency of both methods without compromising their statistical accuracy. The benchmarking results revealed a dramatic increase in performance in both simulated and real datasets. We demonstrated that our Python implementations generated test results matching the original R code, while achieving 380- and 147-fold faster runtimes and 97.4% and 96.2% lower memory consumption on the largest tested dataset, respectively. The Python implementations allow for the analysis of datasets that are significantly larger than previously possible, and enable applications to alternative omics data types and complex statistical models that vary greatly by the number of samples, features, and covariates. Availability and Implementation https://github.com/scikit-bio/scikit-bio

item.title: Bioinformatics: Seumetry: a versatile and comprehensive R toolkit to accelerate high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data. Results Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations. Availability Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry ; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681 . Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Inverse probability weighting-based mediation analysis for microbiome data
item.description: Abstract Motivation Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy (IC) intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounder, antibiotic use. Results To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability-weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of IC intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome. Availability and implementation The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802

item.title: Bioinformatics: Letters and biological process: linguistic structure encodes hierarchical depth in the gene ontology
item.description: Abstract Motivation We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph. Results Semantic representations of term names, combined with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection visualization and k -means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal–Wallis H=5244; p<10−300; η2=.217). Term-name length increased with depth (Pearson r = .34, Spearman ρ=0.37; slope =3.2 letters per level), and this positive scaling held under shortest-, longest-, and average-path depth definitions. Vocabulary entropy followed a bell-shaped diversification–specialization curve with an intermediate-depth peak (maximal at depth 4) that lies outside a Monte Carlo null envelope across most depths, and null-model tests supported a genuine linguistic–hierarchical association. Availability and implementation The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473).

item.title: Bioinformatics: Dynamic graph prior-guided latent adaptation for generalizable single-cell perturbation response prediction
item.description: Abstract Motivation Predicting transcriptional responses to drug perturbations in unseen cellular contexts is a central challenge in single-cell perturbation modeling. This challenge creates a need for models that combine flexible state transitions with structured biological prior knowledge. Existing data-driven models often struggle to generalize across unseen cell types, while many prior-based models rely on static biological graphs without explicitly conditioning prior influence on perturbation-specific target support. Results We propose DGP-LA, a dynamic graph-prior latent adaptation framework that refines biological priors and injects them as gated latent corrections within a cell-state-conditioned transition model. DGP-LA couples a transition backbone with perturbation-conditioned sparse graph refinement. It propagates gene-aligned target support over the refined graph and selectively injects the resulting topology-aware signal into the hidden representation. On Tahoe and NeurIPS, DGP-LA improves Pearson Delta relative to State by 8.7% and 35.8% for generalization across unseen cell types. In zero-shot drug perturbation response prediction on unseen cell types, it improves Pearson Delta relative to CRISP by 79.1% and 67.6%. The model also improves DE-gene recovery, response discrimination, and Hallmark pathway recovery, supporting adaptive latent integration of biological priors for more generalizable and biologically interpretable perturbation modeling. Availability DGP-LA’s source code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/bieyl/DGP-LA and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22155398 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Joint enzyme–reaction retrieval and catalytic optima prediction via multimodal fusion
item.description: Abstract Motivation Enzyme–reaction retrieval prioritizes candidate biocatalysts for experimental follow-up, where recommendations should indicate catalytic compatibility and suitable pH and temperature conditions. Existing retrieval models optimize matching scores, whereas catalytic optima predictors are typically enzyme-level regressors because condition annotations are sparse. This separation leaves ranked pairs unevaluated for condition suitability and optima predictions without reaction context. Results We present GERO, a multimodal fusion framework integrating enzyme sequence semantics, sequence-derived pocket geometry, and molecular reaction representations through feature-gated fusion for condition-aware retrieval and catalytic optima estimation. We define the tolerance-restricted hit rate (Hit@k-TR), which requires both correct top-k retrieval and condition predictions within predefined tolerances. Across enzyme- and reaction-similarity splits, GERO improves Hit@k-TR over two-stage baselines under the primary tolerances. Benchmark examples and an iodinin biosynthesis case study illustrate candidate ranking and assay-condition estimation for experimental prioritization. Availability and implementation Source code is available at https://github.com/ykxhs/GERO .

item.title: Bioinformatics: CMGL: confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning for cancer subtype classification
item.description: Abstract Motivation Multi-omics integration can improve cancer subtyping, but modality informativeness and noise vary across cancer types and patients. Most graph methods for multi-omics data learn modality contributions within the downstream classification objective, leaving predictive reliability for each patient implicit. As a result, uninformative modalities can weaken the fused representation, while unreliable omics can introduce noisy patient relationships into graph propagation. To address these two problems, we propose confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning (CMGL), which produces a separate reliability estimate before fusion and uses consensus patient neighborhoods for graph classification. Results CMGL estimates modality confidence for each patient through evidential deep learning, fixes these values during fusion across omics, and performs classification on an independently specified consistency graph. On four MLOmics cancer-subtype tasks and the 32-class pan-cancer task, CMGL consistently improves over the strongest baseline, surpassing it by 4.03% in average accuracy on the four single-cancer tasks. Its representations recover the PAM50 intrinsic subtypes of breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA), and the model trained on BRCA transfers without fine tuning to kidney renal clear cell carcinoma, stratifying patients into prognostically distinct groups. Availability and implementation The code is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21921069 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: FAMUS: a few-shot learning framework for large-scale protein annotation
item.description: Abstract Motivation Gene function prediction is pivotal in genomic and metagenomic data analysis. Current annotation tools typically rely on the most similar sequence from the referencedatabase and struggle to robustly set meaningful hit thresholds, causing a major challenge for reliable annotation. Results Here, we present Functional Annotation Method Using Supervised contrastive learning (FAMUS). FAMUS compares query sequences to a full array of profile Hidden Markov Models, encoding each sequence’s complete similarity profile, rather than only its top-scoring hit, into a condensed vector space that minimizes the distance between proteins from the same family. Unannotated sequences are incorporated as negative examples during training, enabling robust detection of proteins that fall outside the reference database without requiring user-defined thresholds. FAMUS outperformed KEGG’s native KofamScan for KEGG Orthology annotation and InterPro’s InterProScan for PANTHER family annotation, especially on realistic, sparsely annotated data. We used this approach to build four protein annotation models spanning the KEGG Orthology, InterPro, OrthoDB, and EggNOG databases. FAMUS is a comprehensive, modular framework that supports both pre-defined and user-specific databases. It can be readily integrated into genomic and metagenomic analysis pipelines for accurate, large-scale functional annotation. Availability and implementation All four models are available as a conda package and via our web server at https://app.famus.bursteinlab.org/ , and source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/burstein-lab/famus/ as well as a source code snapshot at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23132542 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Polypharmacological target-aware molecule generation
item.description: Abstract Motivation Designing compounds capable of modulating multiple target proteins simultaneously (i.e. polypharmacology) is critical for treating complex diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. However, AI-driven multitarget drug design remains severely hindered by the scarcity of multitarget 3D structural data and the inefficiency of traditional “generate-then-filter” pipelines. There is a pressing need for scalable methods that can satisfy diverse binding constraints across multiple proteins without relying on scarce structural priors. Results To overcome these bottlenecks, we reformulate multitarget drug design as a sequence-based generation task and introduce PolyTamGen, an end-to-end autoregressive framework. We first curate a large-scale ligand-centric bioactivity dataset from ChEMBL and BindingDB, comprising 1.6 million unique ligands and 4.9 million bioactivity entries. PolyTamGen encodes target protein sets using ESM3, compresses these high-dimensional features into compact tokens via an attention module, and feeds them into a sequence-based compound generator to produce the final multitarget ligands. We further apply Direct Preference Optimization to improve docking-based affinity proxies and drug-likeness. Extensive experiments on dual- and triple-target benchmarks demonstrate that PolyTamGen improves joint success rates over representative baselines while maintaining high chemical validity and diversity. Availability and implementation The code is available at https://github.com/bjzgcai/PolyTamGen . The processed data, model checkpoints, and benchmark results are available at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20594128 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: smiMAD: adaptive multi-view graph learning for paired spatial omics integration
item.description: Abstract Motivation Paired spatial omics technologies measure transcriptomic profiles together with epigenomic or proteomic profiles while preserving tissue context. Integration remains challenging because modalities differ in feature distributions, sparsity, and spatial dependencies. Existing methods may not fully model complementary graph views or adapt spatial constraints, limiting preservation of spatial organization and modality-specific information. Results We present smiMAD for paired spatial omics integration. smiMAD models spatial-neighborhood and molecular-feature graphs through graph-view-specific and common-information branches. An adaptive gate integrates graph-view and modality information, while an alignment–decorrelation objective promotes common-information embedding consistency and reduces branch redundancy. A dynamic spatial-consistency strategy progressively relaxes spatial constraints during training. Across 17 simulated and 15 real RNA–ATAC (assay for transposase-accessible chromatin) and RNA–protein datasets, smiMAD achieved competitive clustering accuracy, spatial coherence, and multimodal integration performance. Molecular marker patterns provided support for the inferred spatial regions. Availability and implementation The source code is available at https://github.com/fdu-wangfeilab/smiMAD , with the version used in this study archived at https://zenodo.org/records/22931624 . Data are available at https://zenodo.org/records/17207079 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: CAD-score-LT: versatile contact area-based comparison of macromolecular structures, interfaces, and binding sites
item.description: Abstract Motivation Comparison of macromolecular structural models requires similarity measures that remain informative for complexes, interfaces, and binding sites. Widely used scores emphasize global superposition or distance deviations and are not designed primarily for direct assessment of contact patterns. A fast and flexible contact-area-based alternative is therefore highly relevant. Results We present CAD-score-LT, a high-performance implementation of the Contact Area Difference score (CAD-score) for superposition-free comparison of macromolecular structures. CAD-score-LT evaluates tessellation-derived contact, binding-site, and solvent-accessible surface areas at atom, residue, and chain levels, and supports selective scoring of substructures, interfaces, and binding regions. The software also provides sequence-guided preprocessing, chain remapping, symmetry-adjusted ligand scoring, local scores output, and clustering. Benchmarking against previous CAD-score implementations on CASP16 oligomer model pairs showed near-identical scores but more than one order of magnitude lower running times, with speedups reaching up to 100-fold for whole-structure scoring and 200-fold for inter-chain interface scoring. Case studies in supplementary material demonstrate utility for large-scale model clustering, analysis of protein–nucleic acid interfaces, and evaluation of protein–ligand docking models. Availability and implementation A repository with the CAD-score-LT software and the reproducible benchmarking and example workflows is available at https://github.com/kliment-olechnovic/cadscore-lt-supplementary-info and archived at Zenodo https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21983528 . The latest CAD-score-LT software is openly available under MIT license as a standalone C++ application at https://www.voronota.com/expansion_lt_cadscore/ , and as a Python library at https://pypi.org/project/cadscorelt/ .

item.title: Bioinformatics: FunFOLD5: combining localised templates and structural homology for accurate predictions of biologically relevant protein–ligand interactions
item.description: Abstract Motivation A central challenge in protein–ligand modelling is to predict not only the presence of an interaction but also the correct ligand identity, binding-site location, and biologically relevant bound conformation. While recent deep learning approaches such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 have demonstrated impressive accuracy in modelling protein–ligand complexes, these methods typically require prior knowledge of the ligand, focus on a single dominant binding pose, and rely heavily on large training datasets. Template-based methods offer a complementary solution by leveraging experimentally resolved protein–ligand complexes to transfer both binding-site architecture and ligand chemical identity, enabling function inference even for uncharacterised or engineered proteins. However, conventional template-based methods are limited by their dependence on global fold similarity, which can miss local binding features critical for ligand specificity. Localised template search strategies may overcome this limitation by capturing conserved pocket-level interactions, enabling more accurate and functionally relevant ligand-binding predictions across diverse protein families. Results We present FunFOLD5, a template-based method for predicting protein–ligand binding sites. Whereas its predecessor FunFOLD4 relied on global fold similarity to identify templates, FunFOLD5 combines local and global searches, integrating rapid structural template retrieval with a local targeted protocol to improve interaction accuracy. The pipeline combines Foldseek-based template searching, curated ligand annotations from BioLiP2, and ligand superposition followed by spatial clustering to identify associated ligands and consensus binding sites. Benchmarking on blind targets from CASP15 and CASP16 demonstrates robust performance across a wide range of biologically relevant ligands, including nucleotides, metal ions, cofactors, and small metabolites. FunFOLD5 achieved high-accuracy predictions for 81.2% of ligand instances (56 of 69). Importantly, the local targeted protocol consistently improved ligand identification, residue-level recall, and binding-pose accuracy. Availability and implementation FunFOLD5 is freely available as a Dockerised pipeline at https://hub.docker.com/r/radiyaman/funfold5_template , providing a scalable and reproducible framework for large-scale protein–ligand interaction analysis and functional annotation.

item.title: Bioinformatics: AutoHMD: scalable and accurate validation of antibody–antigen complexes by heated molecular dynamics
item.description: Abstract Motivation Antibody–antigen (Ab–Ag) interactions are central to immune recognition and widely exploited in therapeutic design, making accurate structural characterization of these complexes a central challenge in the field. While docking and artificial intelligence–based approaches can generate multiple candidate binding modes, reliably identifying near–native conformations represent a key bottleneck. Existing methods depend largely on static scoring functions, which fail to capture the dynamic nature of Ab–Ag interfaces and, as a result, offer limited power to discriminate between competing poses. Results Here, we evaluate heated molecular dynamics (HMD) as a strategy to discriminate binding pose quality based on structural stability under thermal perturbation, implemented through the automated workflow AutoHMD. Across a diverse set of Ab–Ag complexes, HMD enabled clear separation between high–quality and incorrect poses. During simulations, near–native complexes maintained a stable interface, whereas incorrect ones showed progressive divergence, particularly at elevated temperatures. Interaction analysis revealed that high-quality poses maintain more stable and persistent interfacial contacts throughout the simulations. In contrast, incorrect poses display an unstable interaction network. Additional simulation replicates increased classification consistency, while a mean iRMSD cutoff of approximately 2.5 Å achieved 90% accuracy in cross-validation and retained robust performance on an independent external set. Its transfer to Boltz-2-generated complexes further supported the broader applicability of HMD to AI-predicted binding poses. Overall, AutoHMD provides a reproducible, scalable, and high–throughput framework for validation of predicted antibody–antigen complexes, with potential applications in structural bioinformatics and biopharmaceutical design.

item.title: Bioinformatics: hpci improves reproducibility of computational biology research by integrating Continuous Integration with High Performance Computing clusters
item.description: Abstract Motivation The reproducibility crisis in bioinformatics and computational biology can be mitigated by using Continuous Integration (CI), a proven software engineering practice, to automate the testing of analysis pipelines and models. However, the adoption of CI in bioinformatics is limited as existing solutions are typically tightly linked to specific CI platforms, specific HPC job schedulers, or require actions from HPC administrators. Results We developed hpci, a platform-agnostic, open-source utility that integrates CI platforms (e.g. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) with common HPC job schedulers (Slurm, PBS). hpci operates as a standard unprivileged user via SSH, and requires no cluster-side installation. It terminates on the CI runner using the exact same exit code generated by the HPC job, providing feedback to researchers and preventing downstream CI steps if there are errors. We demonstrate hpci’s utility across five diverse computational biology workflows on HPC, highlighting the value of automated testing and continuous analysis for verifying reproducibility in bioinformatics workflows. Availability hpci is implemented in Haskell and is available under the GPL-3.0 licence. Source code and binaries can be downloaded from https://github.com/Garvan-Data-Science-Platform/hpci .Source code is archived in Software Heritage via Zenodo ( https://zenodo.org/records/19587650 ).

item.title: Bioinformatics: PhyloZoo: a unified framework for phylogenetic network analysis in Python
item.description: Abstract Summary Reticulate evolutionary processes (events in which lineages merge, such as hybridization, recombination, and horizontal gene transfer) are widespread across nature but cannot be represented by phylogenetic trees alone. Phylogenetic networks have therefore become an important modelling tool, yet existing software is typically tied to specific inference paradigms and provides limited support for working with multiple network representations in a unified and programmable environment. PhyloZoo is an open-source Python framework that lowers the barrier to developing practical, easy-to-use software for phylogenetic network analysis. It provides data structures and algorithms covering the main representations used in the field, together with dedicated visualization tools and robust I/O for all major phylogenetic file formats. A particular emphasis lies on semi-directed phylogenetic networks, which explicitly represent root uncertainty and have so far received limited support in existing software. By offering a shared, scalable foundation for developing interoperable tools and a combinatorial layer that supports computational proofs and theoretical exploration, PhyloZoo enables reproducible workflows for applied, methodological, and theoretical studies of reticulate evolution. Availability and implementation PhyloZoo is implemented in Python and installable from PyPI, with source code, documentation, and examples available at https://github.com/nholtgrefe/phylozoo .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Correction: From atoms to fragments: a coarse representation for efficient and functional protein design
item.description: This is a correction to: Leonardo V Castorina, Christopher W Wood, Kartic Subr, From atoms to fragments: a coarse representation for efficient and functional protein design, Bioinformatics , Volume 42, Issue 5, May 2026, btag172, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag172

item.title: Bioinformatics: FA-MFMR: a multivariable functional Mendelian randomization method that accounts for correlated longitudinal exposures via factor augmentation
item.description: Abstract Motivation Mendelian randomization (MR) is widely used for causal inference using genetic data, yet most existing MR methods treat exposures as static and have limited capacity to analyze longitudinal measurements. In many biomedical studies, multiple exposures evolve over time, are strongly correlated, and share unobserved temporal structure. Ignoring these features can lead to unstable estimation and reduced power. Results We propose factor-augmented multivariable functional Mendelian randomization (FA-MFMR) for estimating time-varying causal effects of multiple longitudinal exposures. FA-MFMR integrates genetic instruments with functional representations of exposure trajectories and a low-dimensional factor structure to capture shared temporal patterns. By separating common temporal variation from exposure-specific components, it mitigates multicollinearity, improves estimation stability, and accommodates sparse causal structures in which some exposures have no effect throughout the observation period. Simulations demonstrate lower estimation error and more efficient uncertainty quantification than competing approaches, particularly for highly correlated and sparsely observed longitudinal exposures. Applied to longitudinal biomarkers in a Parkinson’s disease cohort, FA-MFMR characterizes age-dependent patterns in the estimated trajectory-level coefficient functions while highlighting uncertainty in localized effects. Availability and implementation The developed R package and code to reproduce all the results are available at https://github.com/YQHuFD/FA-MFMR .

item.title: Bioinformatics: VAEBAC: a representation-learning framework for proteome-scale prediction of amyloidogenic proteins and functional stratification of nucleic-acid-binding proteins
item.description: Abstract Motivation Nucleic-acid-binding proteins (NABPs) govern transcription, replication and genome organization, yet the distribution of aggregation susceptibility within regulatory proteomes remains unresolved. Here, we systematically examine amyloidogenic potential across the nucleic-acid-binding proteomes of four phylogenetically diverse organisms— Escherichia coli , Bacillus subtilis , Saccharomyces cerevisiae , and Homo sapiens —spanning prokaryotes and eukaryotes, to determine whether aggregation-prone sequence architectures are selectively constrained within transcriptional networks. Results Using VAEBAC, a representation-learning framework that integrates large-scale amyloid-family sequences with experimentally validated annotations, we performed proteome-scale prediction of amyloidogenicity across nucleic-acid-binding proteins in each organism. Predicted amyloidogenic proteins were consistently and significantly enriched in Gene Ontology categories associated with regulation of DNA-templated transcription, RNA biosynthesis, and gene expression across all four organisms, a pattern validated using three independent annotation tools. Fisher’s exact test confirmed significant enrichment of amyloidogenic NABPs among transcription regulators in eukaryotic proteomes. Residue-level mapping demonstrated spatial separation between predicted aggregation-prone regions and DNA-binding interfaces, suggesting structural compatibility between regulatory function and conditional aggregation. Experimental validation confirmed fibrillar assembly of selected proteins. These findings support a conserved model in which aggregation susceptibility is functionally stratified across transcriptional regulatory tiers rather than uniformly suppressed within NABPs, a principle conserved across 3.5 billion years of evolution. Availability and implementation VAEBAC is freely accessible at https://www.vaebac.com .

item.title: Bioinformatics: ProDTI: prior-guided positive-unlabeled learning for robust drug–target interaction prediction
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate Drug–Target Interaction (DTI) prediction is critical for drug discovery. While deep learning advances this field, the fundamental lack of verified negative interactions inevitably causes biased risk estimation. Although formulating DTI prediction as a Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning problem is theoretically sound, directly applying PU learning to deep models suffers from early-stage optimization instability and decision boundary ambiguity. Results We propose Pro DTI, a prior-guided PU learning framework integrating domain knowledge into the PU objective. We construct a hybrid prior combining explicit biochemical similarities with implicit semantic representations from large-scale pre-trained models. This prior drives two synergistic mechanisms: soft-label distillation to stabilize the optimization trajectory, and hard-anchor regularization to explicitly penalize reliable negatives and sharpen decision boundaries. Evaluated on five benchmarks, Pro DTI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, exhibiting superior robustness in challenging cold-start scenarios and providing a reliable tool for computational drug discovery. Availability and Implementation Source code and data are available at https://github.com/WangYu-AI4SCI/ProDTI .

item.title: Bioinformatics: HINN prioritizes multi-omics biomarkers associated with cognitive decline
item.description: Abstract Motivation Integrating multi-omics data for disease prediction remains challenging due to the complexity of cross-layer biological interactions and the limited use of prior biological knowledge in many machine learning models. We present the Hierarchical Input Neural Network (HINN), a deep learning framework that incorporates biologically informed connections across genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic layers to model regulatory relationships in a structured and interpretable manner. HINN was applied to blood-derived multi-omics data to predict cognitive assessment scores, including Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale–Cognitive Subscale 11 tasks (ADAS11), and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. A biologically guided feature construction pipeline was used to integrate genome-wide association studies-derived single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), promoter-region DNA methylation, and gene expression data through Gene Ontology Biological Process and KEGG pathway mappings. Results The model was evaluated using a rigorous training strategy that separates feature selection from testing and incorporates cross-validation as well as repeated runs to ensure robustness. Across all cognitive outcomes, HINN achieved the lowest mean normalized mean squared error among the evaluated models, with statistically significant improvements over most baseline methods. Ablation analyses showed that the contributions of individual omics modalities and biologically informed connectivity varied across cognitive outcomes, with the clearest benefits of structured connectivity observed for ADAS11 and MMSE. Feature attribution analysis identified a multi-omics cascade involving SNP (rs116557230), CpG site (cg24041822), and a SOCS4 gene expression probe, which showed consistent associations with multiple cognitive outcomes. These findings highlight the ability of HINN to uncover biologically meaningful cross-omics relationships relevant to cognitive decline. Together, this work demonstrates that integrating deep learning with biological knowledge enables biomarker discovery for complex diseases. Availability and implementation All code, sample data, and instructions are publicly available via GitHub ( https://github.com/bozdaglab/HINN ) and archived on Zenodo ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19197057 ) to ensure reproducibility and long-term accessibility.

item.title: Bioinformatics: Serval: a modular framework for decoding imaging based spatial transcriptomics data
item.description: Abstract Motivation Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics technologies have opened new avenues for studying cellular organization and gene expression within intact tissues. However, the accuracy of downstream analyses depends critically on the decoding step that reconstructs barcodes from fluorescence patterns and maps them to gene identities. Despite a growing number of decoding methods, systematic benchmarking has been limited. Results Here, we introduce Serval, a modular framework for developing and benchmarking decoding methods across diverse spatial transcriptomics platforms. Serval separates key decoding stages into independently configurable modules, enabling flexible integration of alternative algorithms. Using this framework, we develop CoSiD (Cosine Similarity Decoder), a novel method that improves transcript recovery by optimizing cosine similarity to known barcodes. We evaluate CoSiD and baseline methods on synthetic and real MERFISH datasets, showing that CoSiD achieves higher transcript recovery and superior correlation with expression references compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Serval framework generalizes beyond MERFISH. By extending to the DART-FISH platform, we show that CoSiD improves transcript recovery, clustering stability and supports more direct annotation of complex biological structures such as the human primary motor cortex. These results establish that modular decoding frameworks facilitate robust, platform-agnostic benchmarking, ultimately supporting more accurate spatial transcriptomics analysis across diverse biological samples. Availability Serval and CoSiD are open source and publicly available at https://github.com/Roth-Lab/serval . Code for the simulation and analysis pipelines is available from the repositories described in the Data Availability section.

item.title: Bioinformatics: METANet: a supervised ensemble learning framework for reconstructing direct and functional tissue-specific transcription factor networks
item.description: Abstract Motivation Reconstructing tissue-specific transcription factor (TF) networks remains challenging. TF-motif-based methods often lack functional validation, while expression-based methods struggle to distinguish direct binding from indirect regulation. Integration of diverse data types is necessary to accurately prioritize likely functional targets directly bound by TFs across human tissues. Results We introduce METANet (Motif Expression TF Association Networks), a supervised ensemble learning framework that combines TF motifs, cis-regulatory element activity, and linear and nonlinear expression-derived features to predict TF binding. Applied to 36 human tissues, predicted METANet maps significantly outperform established methods in identifying direct, likely functional targets of TFs validated by ChIP-seq and gene ontology. Furthermore, METANet maps capture tissue-specific regulation comparable to existing methods, allowing the identification of reproducible gene–trait associations. Availability and implementation All code and network maps are freely available at Zenodo https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20614479 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: NoiBic: a noise-tolerant biclustering algorithm for high-throughput gene expression data analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation High-throughput transcriptomic technologies generate large-scale gene expression datasets for functional module discovery. However, technical and biological noise can obscure coherent expression patterns and compromise module detection. Noise-tolerant methods are therefore needed to recover meaningful biclusters. Results We developed NoiBic, a noise-tolerant biclustering algorithm for high-throughput transcriptomic data. NoiBic integrates a longest approximate common subsequence-based seed identification strategy with noise-aware column expansion to improve bicluster detection under noisy conditions. Across simulated datasets with controlled settings for bicluster coherency, matrix size, bicluster number, noise level, and overlap level, NoiBic accurately recovered planted biclusters, particularly under noisy and overlapping conditions. Evaluation on bulk and single-cell RNA-seq datasets demonstrated its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene modules and cell type-associated biclusters. Availability NoiBic is implemented in C++17 and available at https://github.com/lcyi0208/NoiBic . The software version used in this study has been permanently archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22732377 . Benchmark datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21919392 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: DeepSAP: an integrated generative and predictive deep-learning framework for controllable design of self-assembling peptides
item.description: Abstract Motivation Self-assembling peptides (SAPs), particularly short sequences whose amino acid composition dictates their spontaneous organization, are emerging as versatile building blocks in biomedicine and bio-optoelectronic materials. As the thermodynamic and kinetic behaviours of peptide self-assembly are affected by intrinsic factors, such as amino acid sequence, length, and hydrophobicity, the controllable design of SAPs with tailored properties is essential to achieve specific structures and functions for various application scenarios. However, existing computational approaches, which primarily focus on prediction or heuristic screening, lack conditional generative capability of SAPs. Results We present DeepSAP, an end-to-end framework integrating conditional peptide generation with predictive screening for property-guided design of SAPs. By pretraining on large-scale peptide datasets and fine-tuning on limited SAP-specific data, the generative SAPGEN model transfers general sequence knowledge to the SAPs domain, enabling the conditional generation of SAPs in low-data regimes. Subsequently, we constructed a lightweight predictive model, SAPBRF, to further screen the generated peptides. Comparative analyses demonstrated that SAPGEN enabled reliable and precise control of the physicochemical properties of the generated sequence, outperformed baseline generative models in terms of efficiency and quality across multiple design tasks. The SAPBRF predictor achieved efficient and accurate screening with high predictive performance. Finally, the complete DeepSAP framework demonstrated strong generalization under unseen physicochemical regimes, where peptides generated and screened by the pipeline consistently exhibited stable self-assembly behaviour, as further verified by molecular dynamics simulations. Our findings indicate that DeepSAP enables the conditional generation of SAPs with desired properties, holding the potential for tailored design of functional biomaterials. Availability and implementation Source code for the DeepSAP model training and evaluation is available at: https://github.com/Paul-hihihopes/Deep_SAP_Design and at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21522690.

item.title: Bioinformatics: BioForge: a fast and safe macromolecular structure preparation library in Rust
item.description: Abstract Summary BioForge is the first macromolecular structure preparation library for Rust, complementing sequence-analysis libraries such as Rust-Bio with cleaning, geometry-based missing-atom repair, protonation, and solvation as a force-field-agnostic preprocessing stage. Across 22 structures (1439–3 819 839 atoms) on a single CPU core, BioForge scales linearly in wall time (fitted N0.89) versus super-linear N1.17 for PDBFixer and N1.25 for PDB2PQR, completing the 3.8M-atom 9MJN in 5.1 s at 1.1 GB peak (PDBFixer: error, 273 GB); PDB2PQR is limited to fewer than 100 000 atoms. BioForge also compiles to WebAssembly for browser deployment and supports direct embedding into simulation and parameterization pipelines via its application programming interface. Availability and implementation An MIT-licensed Rust library crate ( bio-forge ) and a WebAssembly package ( bio-forge-wasm ) extend the Rust bioinformatics ecosystem with structure preparation, both published on https://crates.io and NPM respectively; the same WebAssembly binary powers a client-side web application at https://bio-forge.app that runs entirely in the browser without a server or data upload. Source code and precompiled command-line binaries are freely available at https://github.com/TKanX/bio-forge ; an archival snapshot of the version used for all reported experiments is deposited at Zenodo ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21627953 ).

item.title: Bioinformatics: RAFA: RNA all-atom structure reconstruction from sparse anchor coordinates
item.description: Abstract Summary We present RAFA, a C++ command-line tool for RNA all-atom structure reconstruction from sparse or partial coordinates. RAFA targets settings in which coarse-grained modelling, low-resolution fitting, or partial experimental interpretation provides RNA anchor atoms but not a complete atomic model. The method retrieves experimentally observed 3–5 nt all-atom RNA fragments, fits them to local anchors, combines overlapping fragment-derived coordinate estimates by weighted consensus, and routes sparse and rich inputs through distinct reconstruction paths. In an independent RNA3DB train/test evaluation, no library–test pair exceeded 80% global sequence identity. RAFA achieved lower all-atom root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) values than Arena in 73.3% of target–mode comparisons, with the largest gains in input modes with the fewest structural constraints. Availability and implementation RAFA is available at https://github.com/wangleiofficial/RAFA and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20951205 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: MediNet: simplifying federated and privacy-preserving AI deployment in healthcare
item.description: Abstract Motivation The application of Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning (DL) in healthcare is increasingly feasible in principle, yet remains inaccessible in practice for most clinical institutions. Beyond the well-known challenge of data privacy regulations that prevent centralization of patient records, two further barriers limit adoption. First, deploying a federated learning infrastructure requires substantial technical expertise: configuring distributed training environments, implementing privacy-preserving mechanisms such as Differential Privacy (DP), and managing secure inter-institutional communication demands specialized knowledge that most healthcare organizations do not possess. Second, designing and configuring DL models (selecting architectures, tuning hyperparameters, interpreting results) currently requires machine learning expertise that clinical professionals, including researchers and physicians, typically lack. Existing federated learning frameworks address the infrastructure problem but impose a steep learning curve that effectively excludes non-specialized users. A solution that abstracts this complexity, enabling clinicians and biomedical researchers to design, launch, and monitor federated training processes without programming or machine learning expertise, remains absent from the field. Results To address existing limitations, we introduce MediNet, a comprehensive server–client Federated learning (FL) platform that allows hospitals and research centers to train Machine Learning (ML) and DL models without moving or exposing sensitive data. It offers an intuitive web-based environment that simplifies FL, enabling users to easily select the model and define training criteria while administrators manage permissions and datasets, ensuring granular and autonomous data control. The system automatically constructs and generates the underlying technical configuration (e.g. Python/FL scripts) according to the parameters specified in the GUI. It then orchestrates the secure federated rounds and provides real-time monitoring, fully encapsulating the complexity of deployment and security. MediNet is built upon PyTorch as its primary framework, chosen for its robustness in DL model development along with its Differential Privacy (DP) libraries. Flower AI (Beutel et al. 2020) is used as the federated orchestration system. These underlying technologies are internal pillars of MediNet, essential for ensuring robustness, functionality, and strict adherence to privacy principles. Availability and implementations The general information page for the MediNet software is available at https://isglobal-brge.github.io/MediNet . The MediNet software and its complementary tools are fully available under the MIT license on GitHub. The MediNetHub and MediNetNode code can be found on https://github.com/isglobal-brge/MediNetHub and https://github.com/isglobal-brge/MediNetNode .

item.title: Bioinformatics: STiLE: automated tissue microarray dearraying for spatial transcriptomics
item.description: Abstract Summary Tissue microarrays (TMAs) enable high-throughput spatial transcriptomic profiling of dozens of tissue cores on a single slide. However, existing dearraying methods operate on histological images and do not support the coordinate-based outputs of spatial transcriptomics platforms. Therefore, task of assigning cells to their respective cores (dearraying) remains a manual bottleneck. We present STiLE, a tool for automated TMA dearraying that operates solely on cell centroid coordinates. By eliminating dependence on image data, STiLE is robust to artefacts such as variable staining quality and uneven illumination. The algorithm combines connectivity-based component detection, density-based clustering (HDBSCAN), component-guided cluster merging, and optional grid-based peak detection. Validation on seven public TMA samples (50–150 cores, three platforms) achieved ARI > 0.99, while systematic benchmarking on 396 synthetic datasets with realistic artefacts demonstrated consistently robust performance (mean ARI = 0.992). STiLE accepts standard formats (AnnData, CSV) and is platform-agnostic, supporting diverse platforms including Vizgen MERSCOPE, 10× Xenium, and NanoString CosMx. An interactive Streamlit interface enables parameter tuning, visual inspection, and region-based processing for large slides. Availability and implementation https://pypi.org/project/stile ; source at https://github.com/Huang-AI4Medicine-Lab/stile
